name: Intralesional corticosteroid scalp injection
lead: Intralesional corticosteroid injection places a corticosteroid, most often triamcinolone, directly into patches of hair loss, so that hair regrows in bald spots on the scalp, beard or eyebrows. For people with alopecia areata, regrowth in a visible patch is the way it improves how they look.[1][7]

Wikipedia's article on alopecia areata says steroid injections are commonly used where the hair loss areas on the head are small or where eyebrow hair has been lost.[1] DermNet describes injections into patches on the scalp, beard or eyebrows as a treatment for mild alopecia areata (under 50 percent scalp involvement) that may speed up hair regrowth.[7]

A 2020 systematic review cited by Wikipedia reported more than 50 percent regrowth in 80.9 percent of patients treated with 5 mg/mL triamcinolone injections, while the same article notes that spontaneous remission makes treatment effects hard to judge, with up to 80 percent of people with one or two patches regrowing within a year without treatment.[1]

paras: Alopecia areata causes hair loss on parts of the body, usually the scalp, often as a few coin-sized bald patches, and is believed to be autoimmune, with the immune system attacking anagen hair follicles that may lose their immune privilege.[1] About 0.1 to 0.2 percent of people are affected at any time and lifetime risk is roughly 1 to 2 percent; onset is usually in childhood.[1] In over half of sudden-onset patchy cases hair regrows within a year, and many people have more than one episode over their lifetime, which is why interpreting treatment results is difficult.[1]

The procedure is used mainly for alopecia areata, in small patches and for eyebrow loss.[1][7] DermNet lists it among treatments for mild disease and says injections are repeated at intervals of several weeks and stopped when regrowth is complete.[7] Registered studies also examine it in central centrifugal cicatricial alopecia (CCCA).[2]

The 2020 systematic review cited by Wikipedia found more than 50 percent regrowth in 80.9 percent of patients at 5 mg/mL triamcinolone.[1] Wikipedia states that topical corticosteroids are less effective and slower because they often do not penetrate deeply enough to reach hair bulbs, and that whether steroid injections work for small eyebrow lesions is uncertain.[1] Because of spontaneous regrowth, uncontrolled series can overstate effects, as the same article notes.[1]

Wikipedia lists topical 5 percent minoxidil (a 2019 review found it was more than eight times as likely as placebo to produce over 50 percent regrowth at 6 months), clobetasol or fluocinonide, topical immunotherapy, methotrexate, and JAK inhibitors, with baricitinib FDA-approved in June 2022 for severe alopecia areata and ritlecitinib (2023) and deuruxolitinib (2024) also approved in the US.[1] These are used for more extensive disease than a few small patches.

Local side effects of the injections are not well detailed; DermNet and Wikipedia pages on alopecia areata do not list them.[1][7] Dermatology references on corticosteroid injections more generally describe local reactions at injection sites, which clinicians weigh against benefit.

A registered phase 2 trial combined Restylane and triamcinolone injections for alopecia areata (14 participants).[3] A trial from 2009 compared intralesional botulinum toxin A with corticosteroid injection (20 participants, status unknown).[4] Planned or recruiting trials compare topical calcipotriol with intralesional steroids (60 participants planned) and intralesional triamcinolone with microneedling plus topical triamcinolone (276 participants).[5][6] A phase 4 multicenter prospective study of CCCA treatments (250 participants) is recruiting.[2] The 2020 systematic review of triamcinolone is described above.[1] Published results from these registrations were not found.

card.summary: Steroid injected into patchy hair-loss spots, mainly alopecia areata; reported regrowth is high but spontaneous remission complicates it.
card.note: Prescription procedure for alopecia areata; spontaneous regrowth is common in small patches.

quick.overview:
Small amounts of corticosteroid, commonly triamcinolone, are injected into patches of alopecia areata or eyebrow loss. It is a clinic-administered prescription treatment.
A 2020 systematic review reported over 50 percent regrowth in about 81 percent of patients at one concentration, though many small patches regrow on their own.
quick.mechanism: The steroid acts locally to dampen the immune attack on hair follicles in alopecia areata.
quick.risks: Side effects of the injections are not well detailed. Several registered trials are comparing them with other treatments.

chain: Local immune attack on follicles dampened
angle.text: For alopecia areata, the injection is aimed at restoring hair in a defined bald patch or in thinned eyebrows or beard areas. It is a clinic-administered prescription treatment and is not a treatment for pattern (androgenetic) hair loss.
